subject: AADS
courseTitle: Introduction to African American and Diaspora Studies
courseDescription: Foundations of African American culture from ancient African history and through contemporary issues in the African American experience and the larger diaspora. The characteristics, developments, and dynamics of diaspora culture in the Americas, with a particular focus on the United States. [3] (P)

subject: AADS
courseDescription: Race and racism in the United States and their impact on democratic practices. General intellectual and cultural manifestations of the significance of race and how it influences democratic reform: racial preferences, the prison industrial complex, national security, HIV/AIDS, and elections. [3] (US) (CORE B, C) (LE HFA)

subject: AADS
courseTitle: On Whiteness: Whiteness Studies, Race, and Identity
courseDescription: Key theoretical and political approaches around the issues of whiteness studies, race, and identity. Application of these approaches (and the theories and concepts upon which they are premised) across a broad cultural, historical, and political landscape. [3] (CORE A)

subject: AADS
courseTitle: Curating Black Lives: Imagination, Art, and Global Social Change
courseDescription: Visual arts, social change, and black social movements. Aesthetics, value, and social impact of art and social change efforts. Role of the arts in shaping collective black identity and historical memory of national and global social movements. [3] (INT) (CORE A) (LE HFA)

subject: AADS
courseTitle: History and Myth: Black Women in the United States
courseDescription: Complexities of being black and female in the history of the United States. Interrogation of racism, class, sexuality, and sexism. Black women's multifaceted, diverse community roles. [3] (HCA)

subject: AADS
courseDescription: Race, ethnicity, gender, class and their relationships to both the broader roles of schooling and education in American society. Historical foundation of education for African Americans, educational and socioeconomic inequality, family structures, and social policy initiatives. [3] (SBS)

courseTitle: Special Topics - Beyoncé: Epic Artist, Fem Icon
courseDescription: May be repeated for credit more than once if there is no duplication in topic. Students may enroll in more than one section of this course each semester. [3] (No AXLE credit)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Natural selection and evolution of primates and humans. Theories on early human lifeways and behavior. Bioarchaeological and bioanthropological studies of past and present human health and disease. Evaluation of fossil, skeletal, molecular, and artifactual evidence in reconstructing the past. [3] (MNS) (CORE B, C) (LE SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Seminar in anthropological theory: cultural evolution, cultural history, ethnic relations, cultural ecology, archaeological method and theory, social structure, political organizations, and religious institutions. Repeat credit for students who have earned credit for 3901. [3] (SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseTitle: Coffee: Biology, Culture, and Political Economy
courseDescription: Coffee from bean to cup. Plant biology and pharmacology, agricultural and economic dimensions, and taste and quality. Social and cultural implications of coffee trade and marketing, coffee shop cultures over time, and commodification and decommodification. [3] (SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseTitle: Borders and Territories: The Making of Land and People
courseDescription: Migration, migrants, and the nature and making of borders, from inner cities to international and national borders. International migration and global capitalism. Border conflicts, nationalism, and territories. [3] (INT)

subject: ANTH
courseTitle: Welcome to the Jungle: Amazonia Past Present and Future
courseDescription: Amazonia as focus of international curiosity and colonial exploitation for centuries. Brazil, Peru, Bolivia, Ecuador, Colombia, Venezuela, Guyana, Suriname, and French Guiana. Biodiversity of ecosystems. Indigenous communities, languages, cultures, and histories that challenge the idea of pristine forest. Serves as repeat credit for ANTH 3890 section 02 offered Fall 2024. [3] (CORE C) (LE: SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseTitle: Climate Change, Collapse, and Sustainability in History
courseDescription: The Holocene until 1600 AD. Archaeological perspectives on human society and relation to the environment over time. Historical ecology, anthropogenic climate change, domestication, colonial ecosystems, environmental justice. Case studies of cultures and peoples: Maya, Easter Island, Andes, Norse, American Southwest. Application of ancient innovations to address present concerns. [3] (P)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Time's effects on people and societies. Culturally constituted temporalities; notions of embodiment and alterity. Study of social change; process of innovation through invention and adaptation. Othering non-Western societies as traditional and unchanging. [3] (HCA)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: History, basis in science, and techniques of forensic anthropology to determine general identification and specific identification from physical and skeletal remains. Estimation of age, biological sex, ancestry, and analysis of trauma for medicolegal purposes. Serves as repeat credit for ANTH 3890-01 offered Spring 2024, 3890-05 offered Spring 2023, 3890-01 offered Spring 2022. [3]

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Social histories and contemporary lives of groups often attributed Latinidad through ethnographic texts. Issues of Whiteness, anti-Blackness and anti-Indigeneity with(in) Latinidad. History of "Black and Latino" solidarity. Nation, diaspora, citizenship, race, ethnicity, culture. Afro-Latinidad(es), New Afro-Latinx Movement. Rise of social movements seeking political and social alternatives. Serves as repeat credit for ANTH 3890, section 03 in spring 2023. [3](P)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Public health and social implications of "infodemics"; scientific study of misinformation as form of language and communication in culture and social life; foundations of critical linguistic anthropological perspectives; data-driven and ethnographically constituted analyses of relationships between language, communication, culture, and misinformation. Serves as repeat credit for ANTH 3890-04 offered Fall 2023. [3] (CORE E) (LE: SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Systematic study and analysis of human language. Formation of language sounds, sound systems, the structure of words, the structure of sentences, meaning, language change. Data from diverse languages of the world. [3] (SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Applying artificial intelligence to archaeology. Statistics, machine learning, and deep learning. Hands-on examples from archaeological excavations as well as laboratory studies. [3] (HCA)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Ritual, symbols, belief, and emotion in health, illness, and therapeutic processes. Practices and politics of healing in western and non-western societies, including shamanism, faith healing, ecstatic religious experience, alternative medicine, and biomedicine. Mind-body interactions, medical pluralism, relations between patients and healers, and implications for improving medical care. [3] (P)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Reproductive health politics, with focus on the United States. Role of broader social, economic, and cultural concerns in diverse positions and public debates. How sexuality, race, class, gender, and disability shape experiences of conception, pregnancy, childbirth, kinship, and new medical technologies. [3] (P)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: Methods and approaches in linguistics and cognitive sciences. Exploration of culture and thought, and how culture affects our ways of reasoning, thinking, and behavior. Repeat credit for students who completed 3150W. [3] (SBS)

subject: ANTH
courseDescription: History, theory, and methodology in underwater, marine, and nautical archaeology. Technologies for survey, excavation, and analysis. Cultures past and present, impacts of climate change, and connections to marine resources in the present. [3] (INT)

Portfolio and photographic essay building. History of digital media, sequencing, editing, digital output, and social media platforms. [3] (HCA) (CORE A, C) (LE HFA)

Prerequisite: 1101, 1200, 1201, or 1202. [3] (HCA)

Japan as destination for global travelers. Essential survival language skills. This course is restricted to students with little to no previous experience in Japanese language and who have not taken JAPN 1102 or above. [3] (INT)

subject: ASIA

courseDescription: Southeast Asia's economic rise in the 21st century in relationship to the region's past wars and environmental damage. Imperialism, rubber plantations, waste, trauma, postwar aesthetics, war technology. Course materials in English. [3] (HCA) (CORE C, E) (LE HFA)

subject: ASIA
courseTitle: Blood, Sweat, and Tears in Korean Literature
courseDescription: Critical overview of Korean literature through thematic lenses. Culturally informed readings of old love songs, medieval hero fantasies, modern poems, subversive novels, contemporary K-pop, and webtoons. Violence, modernity, affect, language, genres, media, diaspora, translation, and globalization. Taught in English. [3] (INT) (CORE C) (LE HFA)

[3] (INT)

subject: ASIA
courseTitle: Romancing the Nation in Modern Chinese Literature
courseDescription: From the fourteenth century to the present. Fiction, drama, and poetry. Family relations and nation-state in romantic writings. Knowledge of Chinese is not required. [3] (HCA)

subject: ASIA
courseTitle: Sound and Media in Global China
courseDescription: Sonic expressions in Chinese and Chinese diasporic culture. Late 19th century to present. Cinema, digital media, popular music, and literature. Intersections with gender, identity, and technology. History of sound-based artworks.  Media technology developments. [3] (HCA)

subject: ASIA

courseDescription: Observed and physical properties of stars. Supernovae, neutron stars, and black holes. Our Milky Way galaxy and other galaxies. Cosmology, dark matter, dark energy, and the Big Bang. Serves as repeat credit for ASTR 1015. Corequisite: 1010L or 1020L. [3] (MNS) (LE MNS)

subject: ASTR
courseDescription: Phases of the Moon, colors of stars, shapes and motions of galaxies, properties of exoplanets, and ages of star clusters. Telescopic observations of the Sun. Laboratory ordinarily accompanied by 1010 or 3000. Satisfies the AXLE lab course requirement when completed with 1010 or 3000. Satisfies College Core Inquiry Lab when completed with 1010. Serves as repeat credit for ASTR 1010L.  [1] (No AXLE credit) (CORE: LB)

subject: ASTR
courseDescription: Modern knowledge of Extrasolar planets (exoplanets), discovery methods, benchmark exoplanets and exoplanetary systems. Characterization of exoplanet demographics, composition and atmospheres. Exoplanet science as driven by a revolution in the obtainable precision of traditional astronomical measurements, which have in turn been enabled by new technologies and algorithms. Exoplanets with potential for liquid surface water in our Galaxy. [3] (MNS)

subject: ASTR
courseDescription: Physics of stellar structure and evolution, including nuclear energy generation, equations of state, and heat transfer by radiation and convection. Numerical stellar models. Observational aspects of stellar astrophysics. Prerequisite: either MATH 2400, 2420, or 2610; either PHYS 2255 or 3651; 3200; and either CS 1101, 1103, or 1104. [3] (MNS)
requirements: Prerequisite: either MATH 2400, 2420, or 2610; either PHYS 2255 or 3651; 3200; and either CS 1101, 1103, or 1104.

Topics include current research and industry trends in imaging, regenerative medicine, biophotonics, medical devices, technology and entrepreneurship, and low resource engineering. Open only to first-year and transfer students. Students in the School of Engineering receive open elective credit for BME 1015. SPRING. [1]
requirements: Course open only to freshmen registration group

subject: BME
courseDescription: Structure and mechanics of the musculoskeletal system and the properties and strength of biological materials. Application of Newtonian mechanics, statics, and strength of materials to bone, muscle, tendon, other biological material, and medical devices. Credit offered for only one of BME 2100 or CE 2200. Prerequisite: PHYS 1601, MATH 1301, CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: PHYS 1601, MATH 1301, CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104.

Mathematical modeling and computer simulation of organ systems and physiologic control mechanisms. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 3101. Prerequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104; PHYS 1601. Corequisite: BSCI 1510, PHYS 1602. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104; PHYS 1601. Corequisite: BSCI 1510, PHYS 1602.

No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 3200. Prerequisite: MATH 2300. Corequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: MATH 2300. Corequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104.

subject: BME
courseDescription: Introduction to Undergraduate Research. Introduction to research, either experimental or theoretical in nature or a combination of both, under the supervision of a biomedical engineering faculty member or another faculty member approved by the course director. Students in the School of Engineering may only receive open elective credit for BME 2860. Prerequisites: Consent of course director (see BME undergraduate website for registration details). FALL, SPRING. [1-3]

subject: BME
courseDescription: Introductory laboratory with guided reports. Experiment topics may cover systems physiology, biomechanics, and biomaterials. Emphasis on methods, instrumentation, and equipment used in biomedical engineering. One three-hour laboratory per week. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 4900W. Prerequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104. Corequisite: BME 2301. [1]
requirements: Prerequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104. Corequisite: BME 2301 (Previously BME 2001). No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 4900W.

subject: BME
courseDescription: Mechanics of fluids, heat transfer, and mass transfer in living systems. Basic theories of transport phenomena, applications to mammalian and cellular physiology and the design of medical devices. Prerequisite: BME 2100; MATH 2400 or 2420. [3]

subject: BME
courseDescription: Electronic circuits for measuring and processing physiological signals, analog front-end design, analog-to-digital conversion and digital signal processing. Three lecture hours per week. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 3300. Prerequisite: ECE 2112. Corequisites: BME 3301L and 3400. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: EECE 2112. Corequisite: BME 3301L and 3400. Not open to students who have earned credit for BME 3300 without permission.

subject: BME
courseDescription: Systems-level approach to the design of devices that monitor clinically-relevant physiological functions and variables, driven by the needs of specific pathophysiological conditions. Three lecture hours per week. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 3300. Prerequisite: BME 3301 (2024 or prior), or both 3301 and 3301L, or both ECE 2213 and 2213L, or both ECE 2214 and ECE 2112L. Corequisite: BME 3302L. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: BME 3301 (2024 or prior), or both 3301 and 3301L, or both ECE 2213 and 2213L, or both ECE 2214 and ECE 2112L. Corequisite: BME 3302L.

subject: BME
courseTitle: Quantitative Methods II: Signals and Numerical Analysis
courseDescription: Quantitative analysis and computational methods for biomedical engineering applications. Signal and image processing, numerical analysis, and linear and nonlinear models. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 3300. Prerequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104; MATH 2400. Corequisite: BME 2400. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: CS 1101 or 1103 or 1104; MATH 2400. Corequisite: BME 2400.

subject: BME
courseTitle: Biomedical Materials: Structure-Property Relationships and Applications
courseDescription: Structure-property relationships in both natural and synthetic, hard and soft materials. Bio-inspired materials design, the role of self-assembly in achieving highly ordered structures, material design and properties for emerging biomedical applications, factors influencing biocompatibility, performance of biomaterials in both soft and hard tissues, and biological response to implants. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 2200. Prerequisite: CHEM 1602, PHYS 1601. [3]
requirements: Prerequisite: CHEM 1602, PHYS 1601. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 2200.

subject: BME
courseDescription: Independent research, either experimental or theoretical in nature or a combination of both, under the supervision of a biomedical engineering faculty member or another faculty member approved by the course director. The class meets one hour per week to discuss research design, responsible conduct of research, laboratory documentation, literature review, and scientific writing. Prerequisite: Junior standing, consent of course director (see BME undergraduate website for registration details). [2-3; maximum of 6 hours total for all semesters of BME 3860 and 3861]
requirements: Maximum of 6 credits total for all semesters of BME 3860 and 3861 combined. Will not allow enrollment for students who meet or exceed maximum.

subject: BME
courseDescription: A continuation of the research in 3860 or research in a different area of biomedical engineering. Prerequisite: Consent of course director. [1-3 each semester; maximum of 6 hours total for all semesters of BME 3860 and 3861.]
requirements: Maximum of 6 credits total for all semesters of BME 3860 and 3861 combined. Will not allow enrollment for students who meet or exceed maximum.

subject: BME
courseDescription: Intermediate laboratory with oral and written reports. Experiment topics may include thermodynamics, biological transport, signal analysis, biological control, and biological imaging. Emphasis on data analysis and communication. One three-hour laboratory per week. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 4900W. Prerequisite: BME 2900W. Corequisite: BME 2100, BME 2302. [1]
requirements: Prerequisite: BME 2900W. Corequisite: BME 2100, 2302 (Previously BME 2001, 2002). No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 4900W.

subject: BME
courseTitle: Principles and Applications of BioMicroElectroMechanical Systems (BioMEMS)
courseDescription: The principles, design, fabrication and application of micro- and nano-devices to instrument and control biological molecules, living cells, and small organisms, with a strong emphasis on development of microfabricated systems and micro- and nano-biosensors. Students will lead discussions from the research literature. Graduate students will prepare a research proposal or fabricate a functioning BioMEMS device. FALL. [3]

subject: BME
courseDescription: Advanced laboratory with comprehensive written reports. Students design experiments building on laboratory exercises conducted in BME 2900W and 3900W. Emphasis on experimental design, use of controls, and interpretation of data. One three-hour laboratory per week. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 4900W. Prerequisite: BME 2400, 3900W. [1] (Not offered until 2021-2022.)
requirements: Prerequisite: BME 2400, 3900W. No credit for students who have earned credit for BME 4900W.

subject: BME
courseTitle: Design of Biomedical Engineering Devices and Systems II
courseDescription: Integration of the engineering and life science backgrounds of senior biomedical engineering students through the presentation of design principles for medical devices and systems. Design principles and case examples for biomedical electronics, mechanical, chemical, and computing systems are presented. A full-semester design project is required. Evaluation is conducted through periodic oral and written presentations, and through a final written and poster report. Prerequisite: BME 4950. [3]
requirements: BME 4950  is prerequisite for this course

subject: BRQ
courseDescription: Individual practice focused on the art and practice of Baroque violin, viola, cello, or bass, with emphasis on tone quality, technique, rhythm, interpretation, and literature. [1-2]

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Broad coverage of the biological sciences presenting evolution as the unifying concept. Particular emphasis on basic biological processes in cells and the relationships/interactions between organisms and their environment. Topics include cell structure and function, genetics and inheritance, evolution and diversity, populations, communities and ecosystems, and topics related to biology and society. Not intended for students planning to major in biological sciences.  Not open to students who have earned credit for BSCI 1509, 1510 or 1511 without permission. [3] (MNS)
requirements: Not open to students who have earned credit for BSCI 1510 or 1511 without permission.

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: This pedagogy seminar accompanies a core course in the College of Arts & Sciences and examines the process of teaching and learning of that course content. Students enrolled in the core course lecture may elect to participate in this accompanying pedagogy seminar. This optional seminar will be team-taught by the core course instructor and an education faculty member. [2]

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Central concepts in biology (information flow, evolution, structure and function, homeostasis, emergent properties) contextualized in biological systems at a variety of scales. Development of skills in data visualization and interpretation, experimental design, scientific reasoning, and communication. Prerequisite or corequisite: CHEM 1601. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: An integrative approach to the science of life for science and engineering students. Cell communication. Physiology, organ function and development. Mendelian and population genetics. Evolution, ecology, and speciation. Populations, ecosystems, and conservation biology. Prerequisites: BSCI 1509 (BSCI 1509 waived for students in the School of Engineering) and CHEM 1601.  [3] (MNS)
requirements: Prerequisite: BSCI 1509 (BSCI 1509 waived for students in the School of Engineering) or 1510 and CHEM 1601.

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Alternative to 1511L. Directed research projects with emphasis on experimental design and analysis. Satisfies the AXLE lab course requirement when completed with 1511. Offered on a graded basis only. Prerequisite or corequisite: 1511. [2] (No AXLE credit)
requirements: BSCI 1511 is a pre- or co-requisite to this course.

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly offered as 2205) Evolutionary theory, with emphasis on evolutionary mechanisms. Microevolutionary processes of adaptation and speciation and macro-evolutionary patterns. Evidence from genetics, ecology, molecular biology, and paleontology in the historical context of the neo-Darwinian synthesis. Prerequisites: BSCI 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly offered as 2218) Diversity of plants within the framework of their evolution and environmental adaptations. Biomes from the tropical rain forest to the Vanderbilt arboretum. Prerequisites: BSCI 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly offered as 2219) A structural and functional study of the major animal groups. The problems presented to animals by their environments, and the anatomical and physiological mechanisms by which they adapt. Three lectures and one laboratory period per week. Prerequisites: BSCI 1510 and 1511. [4] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly offered as 2238L) One three-hour laboratory and discussion period or field trip per week. Satisfies the AXLE lab course requirement when completed with 2138 or 2238. Prerequisite or corequisite: 2138 or 2238. [1] (No AXLE credit)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Structure and function of cells, subcellular organelles, and macromolecules. Fundamentals of organelle function, membrane transport, energy production and utilization, cell motility, cell division, intracellular transport and mechanisms of signal transduction. Prerequisites: 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Basic principles and mechanisms of inheritance discussed and related to other biological phenomena and problems. Prerequisites: BSCI 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly offered as 2150) Genetics, cell biology, physiology, and diversity of microorganisms; their role in research and impact on human health and the environment. Prerequisites: 1510 and 1511. No credit for students who have earned credit for BSCI 3234 or 2150. [3] (MNS)
requirements: This course requires BSCI 1510 and 1511 as a prequisite. No credit for students who have earned credit for BSCI 3234.

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Structures and mechanisms of action of biological molecules, proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, and polysaccharides. Enzymology. Carbohydrate metabolism. Prerequisites: Either BSCI 1510 or CHBE 2150; and either CHEM 2211 or 2221. [3] (MNS)
requirements: Prerequisite: Either BSCI 1510 or CHBE 2150; and either CHEM 2211 or 2221.

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Molecular evolution of adaptation and disease. Molecular mechanisms of human disease approached through analysis of evolutionary adaptation in extremophile animals. Comparative analysis of multiple protein systems that facilitate adaptation in some species but are implicated in human conditions such as cancer, visual impairment, and aging. Serves as repeat credit for BSCI 3890 section 02 in Spring 2024. No credit for students who have earned credit for BSCI 5240. Prerequisite: BSCI 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Structure and function of nerve cells. Emphasis on electrical excitability, synaptic transmission, and sensory transduction. Cellular mechanisms underlying simple behaviors, sensory information processing, and learning and memory. Prerequisites: 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: An introduction to statistical methods used in the analysis of biological experiments, including the application of computer software packages. Emphasis on testing of hypotheses and experimental design. Topics include descriptive statistics, analysis of variance, regression, correlation, contingency analysis, and the testing of methods for sampling natural populations. Prerequisites: 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Hands-on analysis of rich biological datasets using MATLAB. Development of programming skills applied to diverse research and analysis contexts within biology. Appropriate for beginner and advanced programmers. Serves as repeat credit for students who earned credit for BSCI 3890 section 03 offered Fall 2023 or BSCI 3890 section 04 offered Spring 2024. Prerequisite: 1510 and 1511. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Reading and discussion of research papers with a member of the Biological Sciences faculty. Registration requires approval by faculty mentor. Prerequisite: BSCI 1510 and 1511. May be repeated for credit once if there is no duplication in topic. Students may enroll in more than one section of this course each semester. [1; maximum of 2 credits total for all semesters of BSCI 3850] (No AXLE credit)
requirements: Prerequisites: BSCI 1510 and 1511. Maximum 2 credits for all semesters of BSCI 3850. Will not allow enrollment for students who meet or exceed maximum.

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Work in the laboratory of a member of the Biological Sciences faculty. Term paper required. Consent of course coordinator and enrollment by arrangement before the end of the previous semester is required. Prerequisite: 1510. Prerequisite or corequisite: 1511. [1] (No AXLE credit)
requirements: BSCI 1510 as pre-requisite and 1511 as either pre- or co-requisite

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Directed student research on a project conceived by a member of the Biological Sciences faculty. Enrollment by arrangement before the end of the previous semester. May be taken only once, and participants ordinarily expected to have overall grade point average of B or better. Offered on a graded basis only. Prerequisite: 1511, one intermediate BSCI course appropriate to the major or 3860, and consent of Biological Sciences 3861 coordinator. [2-4] (No AXLE credit)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Original student research on a defined problem in Biological Sciences and under the supervision of Biological Sciences faculty. Some independence in the design and execution of the problem. Enrollment by arrangement before the end of the previous semester. Prerequisite: 3861, consent of Biological Sciences 3961 coordinator, cumulative grade point average of B. May be repeated for credit more than once, but students may earn only up to 6 credits per semester of enrollment. [2-6] (No AXLE credit)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly listed as 3101; previously listed as MHS 3102, NURS 3102) Continuation of 2101. Structure and function of the human organism. Integration of the gross anatomical structures and organ systems with microscopic structure, physiological function, and homeostatic mechanisms. Clinical relevance of selected topics. Not open to students who have completed BSCI 3101, NURS 3102 or MHS 3102. Prerequisite: 2101. [4] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: (Formerly listed as 3226) The molecular and cellular basis of immunity. Emphasis on molecular structure, the genetic origin of diversity in B-cell and T-cell receptors, antigen presentation, and the cellular interactions leading to the immune response. Tolerance, tumor and transplantation immunity, autoimmune and immunodeficiency diseases, and allergy. Prerequisite: 2201 or 2210. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Molecular structures and biological functions of proteins. Underlying chemical and physical properties. Structural motifs and topology; folding and dynamics; enzyme catalysis; protein-DNA interactions. Structure-based drug design; protein symmetry; supramolecular protein machines. Chemical and spectroscopic methods to probe protein structure and behavior in solution. Prerequisite: 2520. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Mechanisms underlying the maintenance and expression of our genomes. DNA replication, DNA repair, transcription, and RNA metabolism. Students who have completed 4265 require instructor approval to register. Prerequisite: 2520. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseTitle: Advanced Topics in Biological Sciences - Neural Systems
courseDescription: Topics vary; students are expected to have completed one or more intermediate courses in Biological Sciences (prerequisites will vary by topic). May be taken more than once if there is no duplication in topic; students may enroll in more than one section each semester. Offered on a graded basis only. [3] (MNS)

subject: BSCI
courseTitle: Advanced Undergraduate Seminar - Evolution, Science, and Societ
courseDescription: Discussions and papers based on readings in research journals. Topics vary. Prerequisite: completion of at least two BSCI courses at the 2000 level. May be repeated for credit more than once if there is no duplication in topic. Check major requirements for restrictions on total credits. Students may enroll in more than one section of this course each semester. [2] (No AXLE credit)
requirements: Prerequisite: At least two BSCI courses at the 2000-level

subject: BSCI
courseDescription: Open only to majors in the Honors Program. May be repeated for credit more than once, but students may earn only up to 6 credits per semester of enrollment. [2-6] (No AXLE credit)

courseDescription: Individual instruction focused on the art and practice of the instrument, with emphasis on tone quality, technique, rhythm, interpretation, and literature. New students by interview only. Fees apply to non-B.Mus./B.Mus.Arts students. [1-2 variable credits, based on lesson length and repertoire as agreed on with instructor.] Kolkay.

subject: BUS
courseDescription: Ethical issues arising from business and professional practice. Topics will include: corporate social responsibility, employee rights, technology and privacy in the workplace, corporate governance, and globalization. [3] (P)

subject: BUS
courseDescription: (Previously BUS 2300) Emphasis on asset valuation. Stock and bond valuation, capital budgeting, cost of capital, market efficiency, and company valuation. Not open to students who have earned credit for FNEC 2700 without permission, as students will forfeit credit hours. Serves as repeat credit for FNEC 2700. Prerequisite: BUS 1100 (Previously BUS 2100), ECON 1020, and one of BME 3200, ECON 1500, ECON 1510, MATH 1010, MATH 1011, MATH 2810, MATH 2820, MATH 2821, PSY 2100, PSY-PC 2110, or SOC 2100. [1.5]
requirements: Prerequisite: BUS 1100 or 2100, ECON 1020, and one of BME 2400, ECON 1500, ECON 1510, MATH 1010, MATH 1011, MATH 2810, MATH 2820, MATH 2821, PSY 2100, PSY-PC 2110, or SOC 2100. Not open to students who have earned credit for FNEC 2700 without permission.

subject: BUS
courseDescription: (Previously BUS 2400) Accomplishing goals by effectively working for, with, and through others. The units of analysis explored are individuals, teams, and organizations. Not open to HOD or HOS majors, or to students who have earned credit for HOD 2100 without permission, as students will forfeit credit hours. Serves as repeat credit for HOD 2100. [1.5]
requirements: Not open to HOD or HOS majors, or to students who have earned credit for HOD 2100 without permission, as students will forfeit credit hours.

subject: BUS
courseDescription: (Previously BUS 2600) Success in business is driven by providing goods and services that consumers need and want. This course covers how to achieve such success through analyses of companies, customers, and competitors, and making the right decisions regarding what products to offer, and how to price, promote, and distribute them. Course content spans a wide variety of settings including consumer goods, hi-tech, and service firms, and puts a particular emphasis on digital marketing opportunities and the evolving role of social media. Not open to students who have earned credit for MGRL 1200 without permission, as students will forfeit credit hours. Serves as repeat credit for MGRL 1200. [1.5]

subject: BUS
courseDescription: (Previously BUS 2700) Provides an overview of operations in both service and manufacturing organizations. Process analysis, queuing, inventory management, quality management, lean operations, and optimization. Prerequisite: one of BME 3200, ECON 1500, ECON 1510, MATH 1010, MATH 1011, MATH 2810, MATH 2820, MATH 2821, PSY 2100, PSY-PC 2110, or SOC 2100. [1.5]
requirements: Prerequisite: one of BME 3200, ECON 1500, ECON 1510, MATH 1010, MATH 1011, MATH 2810, MATH 2820, MATH 2821, PSY 2100, PSY-PC 2110, or SOC 2100.

subject: BUS
courseDescription: This course covers how to market a brand via the 7 main digital marketing platforms. Topics include understanding the customer experience, selecting and building a digital platform, creating a content strategy, digital marketing vehicles, and assessing performance. Assignments include readings and individual assignments, as well as group work where teams develop and present digital marketing strategies. Students will also earn marketing certifications in HubSpot as part of this course. Prerequisite: BUS 1600. [1.5]

subject: BUS
courseDescription: This course addresses the unique entrepreneurial experience of conceiving, evaluating, creating, managing, and potentially selling a business. The goal is to provide a comprehensive background with practical application of important concepts applicable to entrepreneurial environment. In addition to creative aspects, key business areas of finance, accounting, marketing and management will be addressed from an entrepreneurial perspective. The course relies on classroom discussion, participation, guest speakers, and case analysis. Students will need to draw upon their business education and experience, and apply it to the task of launching a new venture. Students are expected to interact with the business community and actively participate in classroom discussions and exercises. [1.5]

subject: BUS
courseDescription: What makes some organizations more innovative than others? In this course, students will learn how to improve an organization's innovation capabilities. Major themes include how to foster innovation within the firm, how to commercialize innovative ideas through new products and services, how to protect innovation from competitors, and how to overcome common barriers to innovation. Students will also improve their own innovation abilities through a project in which they pitch a new product or service. Note that while we will discuss examples of technical innovation, this is not a tech course; rather, this course is about how to create an effective strategy for innovation in a wide range of organizations. [1.5]

subject: BUS
courseDescription: Sports Analytics uses data and quantitative methods to measure performance and make decisions to gain advantage in the competitive sports arena. Pre-requisite courses have exposed students to powerful quantitative methods such as linear regression and constrained optimization.  These quantitative methods can give operations a competitive advantage.  In this course, students gain further experience in applying quantitative methods to problems in the context of sports.  Typical questions in sports analytics include: How to predict future performance of players or teams?  How to rank players or teams?  Which decision is more likely to lead to a win?  We will cover several sports, but to be able to 'go deep' we will focus significantly on baseball, football, and soccer.  In class, we will analyze real sports data with powerful quantitative methods.  As a result, the course will sharpen students' analytics skills.  These skills are equally useful in many areas of business. Pre-requisites: One of BUS 1700, ECON 3012, or instructor consent, AND One of ECON 1500, ECON 1510, MATH 1011, MATH 2810, MATH 2820, PSY 2100, PSY-PC 2110, or SOC 2100. [1.5]
requirements: Prerequisite: BUS 1700 or ECON 3012 and either ECON 1500, ECON 1510, MATH 1011, MATH 2810, MATH 2820, PSY 2100, PSY-PC 2110, or SOC 2100.

subject: BUS
courseDescription: This course offers a broad overview of the dynamic, complex, and vast world of sports business. Students will explore the economic, financial, legal, and social factors that shape the industry, from professional leagues and franchises to athletes' rights and other emerging trends. Through interactive lectures, case studies, guest speakers, and real-world simulations, you will gain insight into the diverse business operations that fuel the global sports phenomenon. [1.5]

subject: BUS

Students will be exposed to actual commercial real estate transactions and have the opportunity to hone their skills in due-diligence, financial underwriting and investment decision making.  The course will be a combination of lecture and case studies capped with a semester long team project to produce an actual "pitch book" for a potential commercial development. Prerequisite: BUS 2720 [1.5].

requirements: Open only to juniors and seniors.

CS 2123 is not open to students who have earned credit for ECE 2116. Serves as repeat credit for ECE 2123. Corequisite: CS 2123L. FALL, SPRING [3].
requirements: This course required CS 2123L as a corequisite.

Serves as repeat credit for ECE 2204. Prerequisite: CS 1100 or DS 1100. FALL, SPRING. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: Survey of the mathematical tools necessary for an understanding of computer science. Prerequisite: A course in computer science or two semesters of calculus. FALL, SPRING. [3]
requirements: A CS course or Calculus II is prerequisite for this course

Fundamentals: Boolean logic, combinational and sequential logic circuits, information representation in binary form. The von Neumann instruction set architecture, programmer's model of a processor. Low-level programming using the C language, and its mapping to machine instructions. Memory hierarchy and performance issues. Input/output methods and advanced processors: multi-core, GPUs. CS 2281 is not open for students who have earned credit for ECE 2281 without permission. Serves as repeat credit for ECE 2281. Prerequisite: CS 2201. Corequisite:  CS 2281L. FALL, SPRING [3].

subject: CS
courseDescription: Students work in small groups on the specification, design, implementation, and testing of a sizeable AI software project. Projects (e.g., an "intelligent" game player) require that students address a variety of AI subject areas, notably heuristic search, uncertain reasoning, planning, knowledge representation, and learning. Class discussion highlights student progress, elaborates topics under investigation, and identifies other relevant topics (e.g., vision) that the project does not explore in depth. Prerequisite: CS 4260. SPRING. [3]
requirements: CS 4260 is prerequisite for this course.

subject: CS
courseTitle: Error Analysis in Safety Critical Systems
courseDescription: Also listed as ECE 4475. Case study-based course examining errors in safety critical systems, including healthcare and aviation. Errors explored from multiple perspectives, specifically computer science and systems engineering. Serves as repeat credit for ECE 4475. No credit for students who have earned credit for CS 5275 or ECE 5475. Prerequisite: CS 3251 or ECE 3251. SPRING. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: Also listed as ECE 4277. Software issues, secure software design, attacks and detection, identity, sessions, human security mistakes, and security auditing. Serves as repeat credit for ECE 4277. No credit for students who have earned credit for CS 5277. Prerequisite: CS 3251 or ECE 3251. FALL. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: Also listed as ECE 4278. The nature of software. The object-oriented paradigm. Software life-cycle models. Requirements, specification, design, implementation, documentation, and testing of software. Object-oriented analysis and design. Software maintenance. Serves as repeat credit for CS 4278. No credit for students who have earned credit for CS 5278 or ECE 5278. Prerequisite: CS 3251 or ECE 3251. FALL. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: Students work in teams to specify, design, implement, document, and test a nontrivial software project. The use of CASE (Computer Assisted Software Engineering) tools is stressed. Prerequisite: CS 4278. SPRING. [3]
requirements: CS 4278 is prerequisite for this course

subject: CS
courseDescription: Project-based course building on core concepts necessary to architect, build, test, and deploy complex web-based systems. Students form teams, propose project ideas, architect their solutions, and build the initial minimum viable project for their application.  In-class discussions focus on advanced topics in web-development. Prerequisite: CS 4288. SPRING. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: Students work in small groups on the specification, design, implementation, and testing of a sizeable machine learning or deep learning project. Projects can be either application- or algorithm-oriented. Prerequisites: CS 4262, CS 4267, or ECE 4363. No credit for students who have earned credit for CS 5359. SPRING. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: (Also listed as ECE 4375). Design and implementation of embedded computer-based systems. Programming for real-time systems and the Internet of Things. Embedded system modeling, design, analysis, and implementation using real-time and event-driven techniques. A structured project is required. Serves as repeat credit for ECE 4375. Prerequisite: ECE 2218, CS 2201. Corequisite: CS 4375L. FALL. [3]

subject: CS
courseDescription: Computer communications. Network (Internet) architecture. Algorithms and protocol design at each layer of the network stack. Cross-layer interactions and performance analysis. Network simulation tools. Lab and programming assignments. Serves as repeat credit for ECE 4383. No credit for students who have earned credit for CS 5383 or ECE 5383. Prerequisite: CS 3281 or ECE 4375. [3]

subject: CSET
courseDescription: Theory and practice of communicating science to general audiences. Public speaking and communicating in other media. Problems of audience analysis, content, organization, delivery, and language. [3] (CORE A) (LE: SBS)

subject: CSET
courseDescription: Translating technical research for a general readership. Benefits and limitations of different formats, texts, and media for telling stories about science. [3] (HCA) (CORE A) (LE MNS)

subject: CSET
courseTitle: The Trial of Galileo and its Background
courseDescription: The interdependence of cosmological theories and religious teachings from the eighth century BCE to the end of the seventeenth century. Examines scientific works and religious texts, including those of Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Copernicus, Luther, Galileo, and Newton. [3] (P) (CORE C, E) (LE: HFA)

subject: CSET
courseDescription: Exploration and practice of the use of improv in communicating science.  Literature examination of improv as a performance based art form. Practice of improv through in-class games and forms.  Personal reflections on performances. Final performance is a science communication improv show to a general audience. Serves as repeat credit for CSET 3890-01 offered Spring 2025 and Spring 2024. [3] (CORE: A, C) (LE: SBS)

subject: CSET
courseDescription: Examine science and technologies exploited by supervillains to achieve world domination.  Readings and discussions will reveal how these fictional schemes have real-world correlates that pose existential threats to humanity, and students will grapple with how we can summon our inner superhero to address them. [3] (CORE D, E)

subject: CSET
courseDescription: The history and science of food, how it is sourced and processed, and the government agencies responsible for policy. Explores trends in food consumption, nutrition research, and nutraceuticals, and the changing narratives of what is considered "healthy" through an experiential inquiry learning lab. [3] (CORE: LB)
